Use the first print rounded to one decimal percentage point; ignore later revisions, errata, redesigned-table backcasts, or microdata reweighting updates unless Census withdraws the first release on release day and replaces it before the next business day.","dataPointId":"census.cps_asec.spm.under18.poverty_rate.2028.first_print","historicalContext":[{"label":"2021 child SPM poverty rate","value":5.2},{"label":"2022 child SPM poverty rate","value":12.4},{"label":"2023 child SPM poverty rate","value":13.7},{"label":"2024 overall SPM poverty rate","value":12.9}],"drivers":["SPM includes taxes, refundable credits, SNAP, housing subsidies, work expenses, medical expenses, and geographic housing adjustments","TCJA-style extension avoids a large scheduled child tax credit drop but does not recreate the fully refundable 2021 expansion","House-framework fiscal offsets are likely to reduce some transfer resources or raise expenses for low-income families by 2028","Labor-market and wage conditions matter because earnings are still the main resource source for families with children","Shelter and medical out-of-pocket costs can keep SPM child poverty above official poverty even when cash income improves"],"sourceContext":["https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2025/demo/p60-287.html","https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/income-poverty-health-insurance-coverage.html","https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2024/demo/p60-283.html","https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2024/09/supplemental-poverty-measure.html"],"runAt":"2026-06-27T14:22:54Z","reasoning":[{"kind":"heading","text":"Forecast for 2028 Census child SPM poverty under a TCJA House-framework extension"},{"kind":"text","text":"The resolver is the Census Bureau first-print Supplemental Poverty Measure poverty rate for people under 18 in calendar year 2028. This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources include taxes and credits, in-kind transfers such as SNAP and housing assistance, and subtract work, child care, child support paid, and medical out-of-pocket expenses while applying housing-cost adjustments."},{"kind":"tool","tool":"official.lookup","call":"Opened Census Poverty in the United States: 2024 publication page and press release.","result":"Fetched 2024 first-print release date September 09, 2025; 2024 official poverty rate 10.6%; 2024 overall SPM rate 12.9%; 2024 Social Security antipoverty effect 28.7 million people."},{"kind":"tool","tool":"official.lookup","call":"Opened Census Poverty in the United States: 2023 publication page.","result":"Fetched 2023 publication date September 10, 2024; 2023 overall SPM rate 12.9%; 2023 child SPM poverty rate 13.7%; 2023 child SPM increase 1.3 percentage points from 2022."},{"kind":"tool","tool":"official.lookup","call":"Checked Census 2024 poverty report table list for the SPM age table and historical table identity.","result":"Fetched Table B-2 title covering SPM poverty by age, race, and Hispanic origin for 2009 to 2024; fetched Table B-3 covering 2023 and 2024; fetched 2024 CPS ASEC collection year 2025."},{"kind":"tool","tool":"public.lookup","call":"Checked public reporting summarizing Census 2023 child SPM context.","result":"Fetched child SPM poverty rates of 5.2% in 2021, 12.4% in 2022, and 13.7% in 2023; 2023 exceeded the 2019 level of 12.5%."},{"kind":"text","text":"Base-rate/reference-class anchor: after the pandemic credit expansion expired, child SPM moved back into a roughly low-to-mid teens regime. The 2021 value of 5.2% is an exceptional policy year; the more relevant outside-view anchor is 2022 to 2024, centered around roughly 13% to 14% for children when credits are only partially refundable."},{"kind":"text","text":"Level and momentum: 2024 overall SPM stayed at 12.9%, and Census described most groups other than older adults and Black individuals as not significantly changed from 2023. That points to a child rate near the 2023 level rather than a decisive downtrend before the conditional policy shock."},{"kind":"text","text":"Policy mechanism: under the condition, a House-style TCJA extension prevents the child credit from falling back toward the pre-TCJA $1,000 structure, which is poverty-reducing versus expiration. But the extension is not the 2021 fully refundable CTC and therefore does much less for the lowest-income children than the ARPA design that produced the 5.2% child SPM rate."},{"kind":"text","text":"Counter-consideration: if the enacted package preserves more SNAP, Medicaid-linked expense protection, or refundable child credit value than assumed, child SPM could fall toward 11%. Conversely, deeper nutrition cuts, weak employment, or high shelter inflation by 2028 could push the first print above 18%."},{"kind":"math","text":"Start with a post-2022 base of 13.3% from the 12.4% and 13.7% child SPM observations plus the 12.9% 2024 overall SPM signal. Add 0.4 point for partial-refundable-credit limits versus a stronger anti-poverty design and 0.5 point for likely transfer/expense headwinds under the House framework by 2028, giving 14.2%. Use an 80% interval of 10.8% to 18.0%, wider than recent one-year moves because the forecast is four years ahead and conditional on a large fiscal package."},{"kind":"forecast","point":14.2,"ciLow":10.8,"ciHigh":18}]}
